intro:
These exercises all circle one boundary: HTTP, the OpenAPI artifact, and the framework extractors live at the transport edge, and the domain service behind that edge stays free of them. The warm-up and code-reading exercises train your eye to see where transport types have leaked inward; the implementation exercise has you build the calm seam by hand; and the design and debugging exercises move from a single endpoint to the production concerns that dominate the second year of a service: workflow choice, drift prevention, versioning, pagination, idempotency, observability, and graceful shutdown.

The thread running through every answer is that the FastAPI-style feel you want in Rust is not a runtime feature. It comes from types and seams. A request flows in as bytes, decodes into a transport DTO, converts into exactly one application command or query, and only then reaches the service; the result flows back out the same way. When that one-way flow crosses the boundary exactly once, the service is testable as plain Rust, the contract is mechanically derivable, and a framework swap touches only the edge.

exerciseSolutions.title: Map a FastAPI-style endpoint into Rust transport and service seams
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from the handler signature you want a colleague to understand in ten seconds: `create_invoice_handler(state: &ApiState, actor: AuthenticatedUser, request_id: &str, body: CreateInvoiceRequest) -> Result<CreatedInvoiceResponse, ApiError>`. Reading that signature, you can already sort every value into transport-only versus business-relevant, which is the whole exercise.

Which values belong in transport DTOs and which belong in the command. The `CreateInvoiceRequest` body is a transport DTO: it carries only what a client can legitimately send, here `customer_id` and `line_totals`. It deliberately does not carry `tenant`, because the tenant is not something a client gets to assert. The application command, `CreateInvoiceCommand`, is the business-relevant shape: it carries `customer_id`, `line_totals`, and `tenant`, where the tenant is filled in from the authenticated caller rather than from the body. The split matters precisely because it closes a spoofing hole: if `tenant` lived in the request DTO, a client could write another tenant's data.

Which shared resources belong in typed app state. App state holds the things that outlive a single request and are shared across all of them: the connection pool, parsed configuration, the telemetry handle, and, for a create endpoint, the idempotency store. In this chapter's model, `ApiState` holds the `InvoiceService` and a `service_name`; in a real service it would also hold a `PgPool`, a metrics registry, and an idempotency-key store. The reason to make state typed rather than ambient is that the type tells you the handler's true dependencies, and the borrow checker enforces that a spawned task cannot keep borrowing request-local state after the request is gone.

Which checks belong in middleware or auth extraction versus the handler. A request ID and a tracing span must exist before anything else runs, so they belong in outer middleware. Authentication, turning a bearer token into an `AuthenticatedUser`, belongs in an extractor so that an invalid token is rejected before the handler body runs at all. The handler itself keeps only the checks that need the decoded body or the specific operation: the coarse permission gate (`actor.can_create`) and any edge validation of the body shape. Fine-grained authorization that depends on domain state stays in the service.

What the domain service must never learn. The service must never see the HTTP method, the path, status codes, headers, the request ID, or the framework's request type. It receives a `CreateInvoiceCommand` and returns a `Result<Invoice, DomainError>`. The reason is reuse and testability: a service that depends on framework request types can only be exercised through the framework, whereas one that takes a plain command can be driven from a unit test, a message-queue consumer, or a CLI without change.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The four seams: transport DTO, application command, typed state, and caller context, with the HTTP-free service signature noted.
criteria: Transport DTO (CreateInvoiceRequest: customer_id, line_totals) is kept distinct from the application command (CreateInvoiceCommand: adds tenant from the caller).
InvoiceService is placed in typed ApiState with a stated reason (shared, long-lived dependency the borrow checker can track), alongside named production additions like a pool and idempotency store.
Request ID, tracing span, and token-to-AuthenticatedUser authentication are assigned to middleware and the auth extractor rather than the domain service.
The domain service is shown to never see HTTP method, path, status, or the request type so it stays reusable from a queue or CLI and testable as plain Rust.

exerciseSolutions.title: Spot transport leakage into the domain layer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is stated in the starter prompt itself: `BillingService::create_invoice` accepts a `CreateInvoiceRequest`, returns `Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode>`, and has OpenAPI field-example comments sitting above the business-rule logic. Three different transport concerns have crossed into the service.

Which parameters and return types are transport concepts. The input `CreateInvoiceRequest` is an HTTP-facing DTO; it is the shape that decodes from a JSON body, not the shape the domain reasons about. The return `Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode>` is doubly transport-shaped: `InvoiceDto` is a wire representation, and `StatusCode` is literally an HTTP concept, 403 and 422 are not domain facts. The OpenAPI example comments are a documentation concern that belongs to the contract, not to the rule that sums line totals.

Which type the service should take instead. The service should take a `CreateInvoiceCommand`, the calmer boundary type. The handler is responsible for decoding `CreateInvoiceRequest`, attaching the caller's tenant from the `AuthenticatedUser`, and constructing that command. The service then depends on nothing HTTP.

Which type the service should return. The service should return `Result<Invoice, DomainError>`, a domain value and a domain error. `Invoice` is the real entity; `DomainError` enumerates business failures such as `EmptyInvoice` and `Unauthorized`. The handler maps `DomainError` to `ApiError` and then to an HTTP status on the way out. The service never names a status code.

Where documentation and status mapping should live. The OpenAPI field examples belong on the transport DTOs and the operation definition at the edge, next to the router, not interleaved with the summation logic. Status mapping belongs in the handler's `map_err` arm, where `DomainError::EmptyInvoice` becomes a 422-class `ApiError::BadRequest` and `DomainError::Unauthorized` becomes a `Forbidden`.

The concrete benefit of the repaired seam. Once the service takes a command and returns a `Result<Invoice, DomainError>`, you can unit-test the business rule with a plain struct and assert on a plain enum, no HTTP test harness, no router, no serialization. The diagnostic from the hint applies directly: if you could no longer call this service from a message-queue consumer or a CLI because it demands an HTTP DTO and emits a `StatusCode`, HTTP has leaked too far inward. The repair restores the ability to run the domain under any transport.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The leaked service versus the repaired one; status mapping and OpenAPI examples relocate to the transport edge.
criteria: Identifies CreateInvoiceRequest as a transport-shaped input and Result<InvoiceDto, StatusCode> (both InvoiceDto and StatusCode) as transport-shaped outputs that must leave the service.
Proposes CreateInvoiceCommand as the calmer input and Result<Invoice, DomainError> as the calmer output for the service boundary.
Relocates HTTP status mapping to the handler's map_err and the OpenAPI examples to the transport DTOs and operation definition.
States the concrete benefit: the business rule becomes unit-testable as plain Rust and reusable from a queue or CLI, which is impossible while it demands an HTTP DTO and emits a StatusCode.

exerciseSolutions.title: Refactor a handler into a testable service boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A create handler should be boring in exactly four steps: authorize, map, call, translate. The implementation below mirrors the lab and the chapter's `create_invoice_handler`, and it keeps the service API free of any framework request wrapper.

Authorize. The handler takes an `AuthenticatedUser` produced by the auth extractor and performs one coarse edge check, `if !actor.can_create { return Err(ApiError::Forbidden); }`, before the service is touched. This is the authorization or edge validation that the acceptance criteria require, and it runs before any domain work, so an unauthorized caller never reaches the service.

Map. The handler converts the transport `CreateInvoiceRequest` into a `CreateInvoiceCommand`. The crucial move is that the command's `tenant` is filled from `actor.tenant`, the caller context, not from the body. The request DTO and the command are genuinely separate types, which is what keeps the service from ever seeing an HTTP-shaped input.

Call. The handler calls `state.invoices.create_invoice(cmd)` once. The service signature is `fn create_invoice(&self, cmd: CreateInvoiceCommand) -> Result<Invoice, DomainError>`. There is no `Request`, no `StatusCode`, no header map anywhere in that signature, so the service boundary does not accept HTTP request DTOs directly.

Translate. A single `map_err` arm turns each `DomainError` into one API-facing `ApiError` at the edge: `EmptyInvoice` becomes a `BadRequest`, `Unauthorized` becomes a `Forbidden`. On success the handler builds a `CreatedInvoiceResponse` carrying `status = 201`, the invoice ID, and the tenant, which is exactly what a deterministic test, or the lab, asserts on. Because the response is a plain struct of owned values, the test can compare fields directly without parsing HTTP.

The diagnostic from the hints holds: if the domain service still took the request DTO, the transport seam would not be finished. Here it takes a command, so the seam is complete, and the same service could be driven from a test, a queue consumer, or a CLI unchanged.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The four-step create handler: authorize, map DTO to command, call the service, translate the domain error.
criteria: The handler constructs a separate CreateInvoiceCommand from the CreateInvoiceRequest rather than forwarding the DTO.
The service signature take CreateInvoiceCommand and returns Result<Invoice, DomainError>, so it never accepts an HTTP request DTO.
The handler runs the can_create authorization check before calling the service.
On success it returns status 201 with the invoice ID and tenant, matching the lab's deterministic expected output (status = 201, invoice = inv-7, tenant = acme).

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose code-first, spec-first, or mixed OpenAPI workflow honestly
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Given one Rust server, one TypeScript client, and a partner team that wants the contract reviewed before implementation lands, the honest choice is a mixed workflow: Rust DTOs generate the spec, but the spec is checked in as its own artifact and gated in CI. The deciding question, as the chapter frames it, is which artifact is the source of truth, because docs, clients, and server are all downstream of it.

What makes code-first attractive here. The server is Rust and the team is comfortable there. Code-first makes the Rust DTOs authoritative and derives the spec from them, which keeps spec and server mechanically aligned, you cannot ship a handler whose types disagree with the emitted document, because the document is emitted from those types. There is no second source to drift.

What makes spec-first attractive here. The partner team wants to review the contract before implementation. Spec-first puts a human-readable, language-neutral document at the center that all parties can review and approve before anyone writes server code, which is exactly what a cross-team review boundary asks for. Its cost is that the spec and the Rust server can drift unless something forces them back together, and it front-loads design work that a small team might prefer to discover in code.

What the mixed workflow looks like. Rust DTOs still generate most of the spec via code-first emission, but the generated spec is committed to the repository as a reviewable file. CI regenerates the spec from the current code and fails the build if the committed file differs (a spec-diff gate). The partner team reviews changes to that checked-in file in a pull request, which gives them the spec-first review boundary, while the code-first emission guarantees the file always matches the server. The TypeScript client is generated from the same committed spec.

Which workflow makes generated clients least surprising. The mixed workflow, because the TypeScript client is always generated from a spec that is provably in sync with the Rust server and was reviewed before merge. There is no window where the client is cut from stale types.

The CI rule that keeps it honest: regenerate the spec in CI and fail if it differs from the committed file, so the spec can never silently fall behind the handlers. None of these styles is universally superior; the right one minimizes silent drift for the specific teams involved, and here that is the mixed approach because it satisfies both the mechanical-alignment need and the pre-implementation review need.
criteria: Chooses the mixed workflow as primary and justifies it from the team boundaries: Rust server (favors code-first alignment) plus a partner team needing pre-implementation review (favors a reviewable spec).
Names a tradeoff of each alternative: pure code-first gives no standalone artifact to review before code lands; pure spec-first risks server drift and front-loads design.
Includes the CI rule: regenerate the spec in CI and fail if it differs from the committed artifact (a spec-diff gate).
States explicitly that no style is universally superior; the goal is minimizing silent drift for these specific teams.

exerciseSolutions.title: Prevent documentation drift and generated-code drift
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The incident is the canonical drift bug: a handler input field changed, but the checked-in spec and generated client were not regenerated, unit tests passed because they exercised only the handler in isolation, and a downstream team broke. As the chapter puts it, the biggest documentation bug is not a missing description, it is a handler and an OpenAPI contract that silently stopped describing the same system, with no failing test to announce it. The fix is to make the contract part of the build, with at least two checks that have different jobs.

Which check should fail first. The spec-diff gate should fail first. CI regenerates the OpenAPI document from the current handlers and compares it to the committed spec; if a handler field changed and the spec was not regenerated, the regenerated document differs from the committed one and the build fails immediately, before a client release is ever cut. This is the cheapest, earliest signal. The generated-client compile and the contract-fixture test are the second line: if the spec did change, the client must regenerate and still compile, and recorded request/response fixtures must still validate against the schema. Different jobs: the spec-diff gate catches stale specs, the client-compile catches breaking shape changes, the fixture test catches semantic regressions.

Which artifacts are checked in versus generated only in CI. Check in the OpenAPI spec itself, because that is the artifact humans review in pull requests and the input from which clients are generated. Check in a small set of contract fixtures (recorded example requests and responses) as snapshots. The generated TypeScript client and server stubs are produced fresh in CI from the committed spec; checking the bulky generated client into the repo invites accidental hand-edits and merge noise.

How to review Swagger UI without treating it as the only proof. Swagger UI is a real user interface for the consuming teams and is worth reviewing for ergonomics, naming, and examples, but it is for humans. CI still needs machine-checkable evidence: the spec-diff gate and the contract-fixture test assert that the documented contract matches actual handler behavior. Use Swagger UI to judge clarity; use the fixtures and the diff gate to judge correctness.

Which fields and IDs to stabilize. Stabilize operation IDs and the error envelope. Operation IDs are the anchor for generated clients and docs review: if `create_invoice` silently becomes `create_invoice_v2`, every generated client method renames and every downstream diff becomes noise. A stable error envelope (a consistent error shape with a stable code field) means error-handling code in clients does not break when a new error case is added. With these stabilized, downstream diffs stay small and reviewable, which is the whole point: the most useful drift check is the one that fails before a client release is cut from stale types.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# CI: two checks with different jobs.

# Job 1 - spec-diff gate (fails first if the spec is stale):
cargo run --bin emit-openapi > openapi.generated.json
diff openapi.json openapi.generated.json   # nonzero exit fails the build

# Job 2 - generated-client compile + contract fixtures:
openapi-generator generate -i openapi.json -g typescript-fetch -o client/
( cd client && npm ci && npm run build )    # breaking shape change fails here
cargo test --test contract_fixtures         # recorded req/resp validate vs schema

# Stabilized anchors checked in the spec:
#   - operation_id: "create_invoice" (never renamed silently)
#   - error envelope: { "code": "...", "message": "..." } (stable shape)
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two CI jobs (spec-diff gate, then client-compile plus fixture tests) and the stabilized operation IDs and error envelope.
criteria: Defines two drift-prevention checks with different jobs: the spec-diff gate (stale spec) and the generated-client compile plus contract-fixture test (breaking and semantic changes).
Specifies a checked artifact and snapshot strategy (committed spec plus contract fixtures) and a generated-client validation strategy (regenerate and compile in CI).
Calls out stable operation IDs and a stable error envelope explicitly as the anchors that keep downstream diffs reviewable.
Explains that Swagger UI review is for humans and must be backed by machine-checkable contract assertions (the diff gate and fixtures) nearby.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design one production API surface with versioning, pagination, idempotency, tracing, metrics, and graceful shutdown
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The billing API has create, list, and lookup endpoints, one async side-effect path, and an operator requirement that canary rollout and rollback stay safe under load. These are the concerns that do not appear in the first demo and dominate the second year, and each is a promise the contract makes to clients over time. The design below commits to one concrete rule per concern and keeps every rule tied to the transport and application boundaries rather than to framework knobs.

Versioning. Carry the version in the path prefix, `/v1/invoices`, and treat a version as a stability promise: within `v1`, an existing field's meaning never changes and required fields are never added to requests. Evolution within a version is additive only (new optional fields, new endpoints); anything that breaks an existing client's assumptions waits for `/v2`. The version boundary lives at the router, so the application services are version-agnostic and a `v2` can map a different DTO onto the same command.

Pagination. The list route uses cursor pagination, not offset, so a large result set is delivered in stable, bounded pages even as rows are inserted. The edge validates `limit` against a hard cap (for example, reject anything above 100 and default to 50) and treats the opaque cursor as transport state the client must not interpret. Validating the bound at the edge keeps an unbounded scan from ever reaching the database.

Idempotency. The create route requires an `Idempotency-Key` header. The finish-once state lives in app state as an idempotency store keyed by `(tenant, key)`: the first request records the in-progress key and, on success, stores the response; a retry with the same key returns the stored response instead of creating a second invoice. This is the rule that makes the async side-effect path safe to retry, the side effect fires once per key even if the client or a load balancer retries.

Trace and metric fields before rollout. Every request gets a request ID and a trace ID, both established in outer middleware before auth runs, and both attached to the tracing span and to log lines. Metrics include route label, status class, and request latency; for the async side-effect path, also publish queue age (how long a job waited) and publish latency (how long the side effect took). These give an operator the signal to judge a canary: if the canary's latency or queue age regresses, roll back. Request ID and trace ID are the minimum two observability hooks; queue age and publish latency cover the async path.

Graceful shutdown. On a shutdown signal the server first stops admitting new requests (close the listener / fail readiness so the load balancer drains it), then waits for in-flight handlers to finish within a bounded deadline, then flushes the async side-effect path so no enqueued job is dropped, and only then exits. The ordering is the point: admission stops before exit. If the service kept accepting requests or dropped queued side effects during deploy shutdown, it would produce duplicate or lost side effects, and the shutdown was not actually graceful. As the hint says, a production API design is an ownership and pacing design once traffic is real.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One concrete rule per production concern: path versioning, edge-validated cursor pagination, keyed idempotency, named telemetry fields, and an admission-stops-first shutdown.
criteria: States one versioning rule (path-prefixed /v1, additive-only within a version), one pagination rule (cursor pagination with an edge-validated limit cap), and one idempotency rule (Idempotency-Key with finish-once state in app state).
Includes more than two observability hooks: request ID and trace ID, plus route, latency, queue age, and publish latency on the async path.
Describes a shutdown sequence that stops admission first, then drains in-flight handlers, then flushes the side-effect path, then exits.
Ties each rule to transport and application boundaries (router-level versioning, edge validation, idempotency store in typed state) rather than to framework settings alone.

labSolution.explanation:
The program models the chapter's central seam without any web framework, so it compiles with the standard library alone. There are two distinct input shapes: `CreateInvoiceRequest` is the transport DTO (only `customer_id` and `line_totals`, the fields a client may send), and `CreateInvoiceCommand` is the application command, which additionally carries `tenant`. The `InvoiceService::create_invoice` method takes only the command and returns `Result<Invoice, DomainError>`; it names no HTTP type, which is what makes the domain layer testable as plain Rust.

The `create_invoice_handler` function is the single place that knows about both HTTP and the domain. It runs the four steps in order: it authorizes (`actor.can_create`), maps the DTO into a command while filling `tenant` from the authenticated caller rather than the body, calls the service once, and translates `DomainError` into `ApiError` at the edge. On success it builds a `CreatedInvoiceResponse` with `status = 201`.

In `main`, the actor's tenant is `acme` and the request's `customer_id` is `"7"`. The service computes `total_cents` as 1200 + 3000 = 4200 and sets `id` to `format!("inv-{}", "7")`, which is `inv-7`. The handler returns a 201 response whose tenant is copied from the caller context. The three `println!` calls then emit `status = 201`, `invoice = inv-7`, and `tenant = acme`, matching the expected output exactly. The compiled binary was run and its stdout matched the expected output character for character.

reviewAnswers.question: What does it mean for a domain service to stay HTTP-free in a Rust web application?
reviewAnswers.answer: It means the service's signatures name no transport concepts: it takes an application command or query and returns a domain value and a domain error (for example `Result<Invoice, DomainError>`), never a framework request type, a status code, or a wire DTO. HTTP DTOs, extractors, and the OpenAPI artifact live at the transport edge, and the handler is the only code that translates between that edge and the command. The practical test is that the same service could run unchanged behind a message-queue consumer or a CLI; if it could not, HTTP has leaked too far inward and the service is no longer testable as plain Rust.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are typed extractors and typed state a better long-term seam than passing one raw request object around?
reviewAnswers.answer: Typed extractors decode exactly the parts a handler needs, the path, the body, the authenticated caller, into named types, so the handler signature documents its true dependencies and an invalid token or malformed body is rejected before the handler body runs. Typed state names the shared, long-lived dependencies (pool, config, telemetry, idempotency store) explicitly, and the borrow checker enforces that a spawned task cannot keep borrowing request-local state after the request is gone. A single raw request object hides all of this behind one opaque value, invites ambient assumptions about what is present, and makes the ownership model impossible for the compiler to verify.

reviewAnswers.question: When is code-first OpenAPI the calm default, and when does spec-first become more honest?
reviewAnswers.answer: Code-first is the calm default when the Rust server is the source of truth and the team mostly needs the spec to stay mechanically aligned with the handlers, since deriving the spec from the DTOs means the two cannot disagree. Spec-first becomes more honest when a contract must be reviewed and approved by another team before implementation lands, because a language-neutral document is what a cross-team review boundary actually needs. In practice a mixed workflow is often the most honest: emit the spec from code, but check it in and gate it in CI so it is both mechanically aligned and reviewable, with the goal always being to minimize silent drift for the specific teams involved rather than to pick the theoretically purest style.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should generated clients stay in the transport layer rather than in the domain layer?
reviewAnswers.answer: A generator encodes its own opinions about naming, optionality, and error shape, and those opinions will not match your domain's, so letting generated types reach into business logic couples the domain to a tool's conventions and to the wire format. Keeping generated clients and types at the transport boundary means the domain model stays expressed in its own terms, and a regenerated client (after a spec change) only forces edits at the edge, not throughout the core. This is the same boundary rule applied to the consuming side: transport code, generated or hand-written, translates into and out of domain commands and values but never becomes the domain.

reviewAnswers.question: What CI checks keep Swagger UI and generated SDKs from silently drifting away from handler behavior?
reviewAnswers.answer: The first and cheapest is a spec-diff gate: regenerate the OpenAPI document from the current handlers in CI and fail the build if it differs from the committed spec, so a stale spec is caught before any client is cut from it. Backing that, regenerate the client SDK from the committed spec and require it to compile (catching breaking shape changes), and run contract-fixture tests where recorded requests and responses are validated against the schema (catching semantic regressions). Stabilizing operation IDs and the error envelope keeps downstream diffs small and reviewable, and because Swagger UI is for humans, these machine-checkable assertions, not the rendered docs, are what prove the contract still matches handler behavior.
